source_text: Proinde incarnatio Christi opus suae divinitatis tuetur, qui afferens ad me naturam meam et voluntatem suam, cuius mihi speculum offerebat et regulam, pronuntiansque nihil in se diabolum invenisse peccati, ostendit culpam non de carnis conditu, sed de sola suscipi voluntate. Denique ut nusquam in Scripturis legitur Christum fugisse peccatum, quod a nascentibus trahi nosset; ita etiam illud claro testimonio perdocetur, quod suscepti hominis iustitia non de naturae diversitate, sed de voluntaria actione substiterit.
pass_a_gloss: Accordingly the incarnation of Christ protects the work of his divinity, who bringing to me my nature and his will, of which he was offering me a mirror and a rule, and pronouncing that the devil had found nothing of sin in him, showed that fault is to be taken up not from the founding of the flesh but from will alone. Finally as nowhere in the Scriptures is it read that Christ fled a sin which he knew is drawn from those being born; so also that is thoroughly taught by clear testimony, that the justice of the assumed human stood not from a diversity of nature but from voluntary action.

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Thus Christ’s incarnation defends the work of his own divinity. He brought to me my nature and his own will, offering that will as a mirror and a rule for me. By declaring that the devil had found no sin in him, he showed that guilt is acquired not from the flesh’s creation but solely from the will (compare John 14:30). Nowhere in Scripture do we read that Christ escaped a sin he knew was inherited at birth. Rather, clear testimony fully teaches that the righteousness of the humanity he assumed rested not on a difference of nature but on voluntary action.

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.
